section.title: Matthias Chosen
section.sectionRationale: Between the ascension and Pentecost, the waiting church devotes itself to prayer. Peter, reading the fall of Judas in light of Scripture, leads the believers to fill the vacant place among the Twelve. Two men are proposed, the church prays for God to show His choice, and the lot falls to Matthias, restoring the apostolic circle of witnesses before the Spirit comes.
section.thesis: The waiting church prays as one, and, guided by Scripture and by God who knows every heart, restores the circle of apostolic witnesses so that the number chosen to testify to the risen Christ is complete before Pentecost.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the gathered church waiting in united prayer; Peter's reading of Judas's fall through the Psalms and the need for a replacement witness; and the prayerful choice of Matthias by lot to complete the Twelve.

units.label: The waiting church at prayer
units.note: with one accord, continually in prayer

verses.text: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, which is near the city, a Sabbath day’s journey away.

When they arrived, they went to the upper room where they were staying: Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James.
With one accord they all continued in {{proseuche|prayer}}, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with His brothers.

units.label: Peter reads Judas's fall through Scripture
units.note: the Scripture had to be fulfilled

verses.text: In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (a gathering of about a hundred and twenty) and said,
“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled that the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide for those who arrested Jesus.
He was one of our number and shared in this {{diakonia|ministry}}.”
(Now with the reward for his wickedness Judas bought a field; there he fell headlong and burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out.
This became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so they called that field in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)
“For it is written in the book of Psalms: ‘May his place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in it,’ and, ‘May another take his position.’

units.label: Matthias chosen to complete the Twelve
units.note: a witness with us of His resurrection

verses.text: Therefore it is necessary to choose one of the men who have accompanied us the whole time the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,
beginning from John’s baptism until the day Jesus was taken up from us. For one of these must become a {{martys|witness}} with us of His resurrection.”
So they proposed two men: Joseph called Barsabbas (also known as Justus) and Matthias.
And they prayed, “Lord, You know everyone’s heart. Show us which of these two You have chosen
to take up this ministry and apostleship, which Judas abandoned to go to his rightful place.”
Then they cast {{kleros|lots}}, and the lot fell to Matthias. So he was added to the eleven apostles.

proseuche.gloss: Prayer, especially prayer addressed to God. The waiting church devotes itself with one accord to prayer as it awaits the promised Spirit. Prayer marks the newborn community from the first and frames every major step, including the choice of Matthias.

diakonia.gloss: Service, ministry, the work of a servant. Judas had shared in this ministry and then abandoned it; the vacant place is described as a ministry and apostleship to be taken up. The apostolic office is not status but service in the cause of Christ.

martys.gloss: Witness, one who testifies to what he has seen. The essential qualification for the replacement is that he accompanied Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension, so he can be a witness with the others of the resurrection. Apostolic testimony rests on eyewitness experience of the risen Christ.

kleros.gloss: A lot, or the portion assigned by lot. Casting lots was an Old Testament way of seeking God's decision, trusting Him to direct the outcome. This is the last time Scripture records the practice; after Pentecost the church is led by the indwelling Spirit.

basic.context: After Jesus is taken up, the disciples return to Jerusalem and gather in an upper room. About a hundred and twenty believers wait together, devoting themselves to prayer. During this waiting, Peter stands up to address a problem: Judas, one of the Twelve, has fallen away and died. Peter shows from the Psalms that his place should be filled, and the church chooses Matthias to complete the circle of apostolic witnesses before Pentecost.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the church's obedient, prayerful preparation for the Spirit. The main questions are: why does the number twelve matter, what qualifies an apostle, and how should we understand the casting of lots? Notice how Peter reasons from Scripture and how the church submits the decision to God, who knows every heart, rather than to mere human preference.
basic.originalLanguages: The believers continue in proseuche, prayer, with one accord. Judas had shared in the diakonia, the ministry, and abandoned it. The replacement must be a martys, a witness, of the resurrection. And the church discerns God's choice by kleros, the casting of lots, trusting Him to direct the outcome.
basic.typology: The twelve apostles answer to the twelve tribes of Israel; Jesus is reconstituting the people of God around Himself. Judas's betrayal and the filling of his place echo the psalms of the righteous sufferer, David foreshadowing the greater Son. The eyewitness testimony required here anchors the church on the historical reality of the risen Christ.
basic.christ: The whole concern is to secure witnesses to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. The apostolic office exists to testify to Him. Even Judas's tragic fall is read as fulfilling the Scripture that the Holy Spirit spoke through David, showing that the events around Christ were within God's foreknown plan.
basic.god: The church prays to the Lord who knows everyone's heart and asks Him to show His choice. God is the one who selects His servants; the believers simply seek and submit to His will. Their united prayer and their trust that God directs the lot reveal a community that leans on God for every step.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 69 and Psalm 109 supply the texts Peter cites about Judas. Luke 6 records Jesus choosing the original Twelve. Proverbs 16 teaches that the lot is cast but its decision is from the Lord. Acts 6 shows the church again praying as it appoints servants for ministry.
basic.oneStory: Before the Spirit is poured out, the church completes the band of eyewitnesses who will carry the good news. This small, prayerful scene prepares the ground for Pentecost and for the mission that will run from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, all resting on faithful testimony to the risen Christ.

context.literary:
Acts 1:12 to 26 is the bridge between the ascension and Pentecost, and Luke builds it as three small panels. The first, verses 12 to 14, is a list: the place, the eleven by name, the women, Mary and the brothers of Jesus, all 'with one accord' in prayer. The second, verses 15 to 22, is Peter's speech, with a parenthesis in verses 18 and 19 on Judas's end, which most readers take as Luke's own aside to his reader and not part of what Peter said, since it speaks of what 'they called that field in their own language.' The third, verses 23 to 26, is the action: two nominated, a prayer, the lot, and Matthias numbered with the eleven.

The list of names in verse 13 follows the order of Luke 6:14 to 16 with small changes, and the list stops at eleven. That omission is the problem the whole passage exists to solve. Luke is a careful structurer, and the gap in the list of the Twelve is the narrative wound that the passage heals before the Spirit comes.

Peter's speech has a clear logic, and Luke signals it with the two words that carry the argument. In verse 16 the Scripture 'had to be fulfilled,' and in verse 21 it is 'necessary' to choose another. The same Greek verb of divine necessity, dei, governs both. The first necessity concerns the past, what had to happen to Judas, and the second concerns the present, what the church now has to do. Luke wants the reader to see that obedience follows from understanding what God has said.

The passage also begins and ends with a sense of place. It starts at the Mount of Olives and ends with 'his rightful place,' verse 25, where Judas has gone, while the new apostle takes up the ministry Judas abandoned. The word 'place' (topos) turns up twice in verse 25: the place in the ministry that Judas abandoned, and the place to which he went.
context.historical:
The upper room, hyperoon in Greek, was an upstairs chamber of the kind used for gatherings in a larger house. Where it stood is not stated, and Luke does not say that it was the room of the Last Supper, though some have thought so. About a hundred and twenty people gathered in the days between the ascension and Pentecost, which is the number Luke gives in verse 15.

The inclusion of women and of Jesus' brothers is historically striking. During His ministry His brothers did not believe in Him, John 7:5, but Paul records that the risen Lord appeared to James, 1 Corinthians 15:7, and here they are praying with the believers. The women who had followed Him from Galilee, Luke 8:1 to 3, and Mary herself are named among the community.

The apostles' role is shaped by Jewish ideas of agency, in which a sent person represents the sender fully, and by the pattern of twelve. Jesus had chosen Twelve from a larger group of disciples, Luke 6:13, and had told them that they would sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel, Luke 22:30. In Israel's history twelve tribes descended from Jacob's sons, and the appointment of Twelve in the ministry of Jesus signalled the reconstitution of Israel around Himself. A vacancy in the Twelve left the symbol incomplete as the new age began.

Casting lots was an accepted way of reaching a decision in Israel. It was used to divide the land, Numbers 26:55 and Joshua 18:6, to identify wrongdoing, Joshua 7:14 to 18, to assign priestly duties, 1 Chronicles 24:5 and Luke 1:9, and to settle disputes, Proverbs 18:18. Lots were thrown in a way that left the outcome to God. The apostles are using a familiar tool, in a way that suited the Old Testament era they stood at the end of, and with a prayer that makes their dependence plain.
context.canonical:
Peter reads two psalms of David as bearing on Judas. The first is from Psalm 69:25, 'May their place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in their tents,' which he applies in the singular to Judas, and the second is Psalm 109:8, 'May his days be few; may another take his position.' Both are psalms of a righteous sufferer, and both were already used of Jesus in the Gospels, since Psalm 69:9 is applied to Him in John 2:17 and Psalm 69:21 stands behind the vinegar of the cross, John 19:28 to 30. Peter reads them as texts about the enemy of David's greater Son, a pattern in which the righteous sufferer's enemies share the fate foretold.

The call of the Twelve in the Gospels, Mark 3:13 to 19 and Luke 6:12 to 16, supplies the background, and the promise of Luke 22:28 to 30 shows what is at stake. The Twelve are mentioned again in Acts 6:2, where 'the Twelve' summon the disciples, and in 1 Corinthians 15:5, where Paul says the risen Lord appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve, which shows that Matthias was counted. The last chapters of Scripture give the symbol its end, since the wall of the new Jerusalem has twelve foundations bearing 'the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb,' Revelation 21:14.

The prayer of verse 24 echoes a long tradition. 'You know everyone's heart' recalls Solomon's prayer, 1 Kings 8:39, and God's word to Samuel that He looks at the heart, 1 Samuel 16:7. It is taken up again at Acts 15:8, where God who knows the heart shows His approval by giving the Spirit to the Gentiles. And the Proverb that the lot is cast into the lap but its decision is from the LORD, Proverbs 16:33, gives the theology of the act.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see the church as an orderly, Scripture shaped community that acts in dependence on God. Before Pentecost they have not yet been given power, yet they already know what to do: pray, read the Scriptures and act on what they learn. Luke shows no frantic improvisation. A community of a hundred and twenty is guided by the word of God and by the prayer of the whole body, and a leader, Peter, who has been restored after his denial, takes up a responsible role.

He also wants to establish the limits of the apostolic office. The qualifications in verses 21 and 22 are specific: someone who has been with them from John's baptism to the ascension, and who can be a witness of the resurrection. The office is about testimony, and the testimony depends on having seen. By stating the criteria, Luke protects the church's claim that its message rests on first hand witness of the risen Christ, which is his purpose in the whole book, Luke 1:2.

Finally, Luke tells the story of Judas honestly, as part of what happened. Judas's end is described bluntly, and the lesson is drawn at once: even this betrayal is within what the Scripture foretold, and the loss does not cripple the church. The community moves from the grief of a fallen member to the restoration of the circle.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what the church did in a particular moment before the Spirit was given. It does not establish the casting of lots as a method that believers must use. After Pentecost Luke never again records anyone using it. Decisions are made through the Spirit's guidance, Acts 13:2, through discussion and agreement, Acts 15:28, and through the congregation's choice of men 'full of the Spirit and wisdom,' Acts 6:3. The lot belongs to the end of the older era, and what is prescriptive is the posture: prayer, Scripture and submission to the Lord who knows hearts.

The passage does not command the church to replace every apostle or to appoint successors in the Twelve. When James the brother of John was killed in Acts 12:2, no one was appointed in his place. The Twelve are a unique group of witnesses, and their number serves a symbolic purpose. The pattern that does carry forward is that leadership is set on the foundation of the testimony they gave.

The graphic account of Judas's death is description, and the quotations from the Psalms are Peter's interpretation of events, not a licence to read every psalm of cursing as a prediction about a specific person.

debates.question: How do Acts 1:18 and Matthew 27:5 to 8 fit together on Judas's death?

views.label: The accounts are complementary
views.case: Matthew says Judas threw the silver into the temple, hanged himself, and that the priests then used the money to buy the Potter's Field. Acts says Judas bought a field with the reward for his wickedness and fell headlong, bursting open. A common harmonisation is that Judas hanged himself, the body fell or was later cut down and burst open, and the priests' purchase was counted as his since it was his money. The two share the key facts: the money, the field, the name Field of Blood, and a violent death.

views.label: The accounts are independent traditions
views.case: Others say the two writers drew on separate accounts of a shocking event, each emphasising different things. The differences are not resolved by guesses, and Luke and Matthew each have their own theological purpose, Matthew linking the field to Jeremiah and Zechariah, and Luke linking it to the psalms.

debates.bearing: The agreement of the two accounts on the main points is strong. The disagreement over details is not a reason to doubt the death of Judas or the fulfilment of Scripture, and Luke's interest is the lesson: that the place of Judas needed to be filled.

debates.question: Was Matthias the right choice, or was Paul the twelfth apostle?

views.label: Matthias was rightly chosen
views.case: Luke tells the story without a word of criticism, calls him one of 'the eleven' and counts him with them, and later speaks of 'the Twelve' in Acts 6:2. The procedure follows Scripture and prayer, and the Lord answered. The Twelve are mentioned again as a group in 1 Corinthians 15:5, after Judas's death.

views.label: Paul was the Lord's choice
views.case: Some have suggested that Peter acted too quickly, before the Spirit came, and that Paul was the apostle the Lord had in mind. They note that Matthias is never mentioned again in Acts. The text does not hint at this, and Paul himself says he is the 'least of the apostles,' 1 Corinthians 15:9, and describes his own call as unusual, not as a replacement.

views.label: The question over-reads the silence
views.case: Many others observe that Acts says little about most of the Twelve after the opening chapters, so silence about Matthias proves nothing. The criteria of verses 21 and 22 can be argued as met by Matthias, and Paul's apostleship is a different kind, a calling to the Gentiles after the ascension.

debates.bearing: The text supports the first view. Luke's own presentation is positive, and the claim that Paul replaced Judas requires an argument from silence. Paul's apostleship stands on its own ground.

debates.question: Should believers decide matters by lot today?

views.label: No, because the practice belonged to the earlier era
views.case: Acts records the lot only here, before the Spirit came. After Pentecost the church relies on the Spirit's guidance, wisdom and counsel. The apostles used the lot while Jesus was ascended and the Spirit had not yet been given.

views.label: Yes in principle, if the posture is the same
views.case: A few hold that nothing in Scripture forbids the practice, and Proverbs 16:33 affirms that God directs the outcome. They say it can be useful when a choice is between equally qualified candidates.

debates.bearing: Most agree that what the passage models is the dependence and not the device: prayer to the Lord who knows hearts, and willingness to accept His answer.

study.originalLanguages:
The key word of the prayer is kardiognostes, 'heart knower,' in 'Lord, You know everyone's heart,' verse 24. It is a compound of kardia, heart, and a word for knowing, and it appears in the New Testament here and again in Acts 15:8, where God 'who knows the heart' approves the Gentiles. The prayer is addressed to the 'Lord,' and since the question is about whom He has chosen, the natural reading is that the Lord Jesus, who chose the Twelve, Luke 6:13, is asked to show His choice. The verb used for 'show,' anadeixon, is the one used of Jesus appointing the seventy-two in Luke 10:1, a verbal link that supports this reading.

Luke plays on the word kleros. In verse 17 Judas 'shared in this ministry,' which in the Greek is closer to 'received the lot of this ministry,' a share allotted to him. In verse 26 the apostles 'cast lots,' using the plural of the same word, and 'the lot fell,' and the allotment passes to another. The word covers an object used for a decision, the decision itself and the share it gives, and Luke lets the three meanings echo. The Greek Old Testament uses kleros also for Israel's inheritance, so the word carries a sense of a gift from God, not a prize earned.

The word for ministry is diakonia, service, and 'apostleship' in verse 25 is apostole, a commission. The verse joins them: the position is a service and a sending. Judas 'abandoned' it, a verb that means to turn aside or fall away, and went 'to his rightful place,' idion topon, his own place, a phrase that makes the end of Judas the consequence of his own choice and not an arbitrary fate.

The requirement of verse 21 that the man had been with them as the Lord Jesus 'went in and out among us' uses an idiom for the whole of a person's public life, found in the Old Testament in Numbers 27:17, where a leader 'goes out and comes in before' the people. The phrase means they had shared the daily life of the ministry, from John's baptism onward.

The quotation in verse 20 differs slightly from the psalm as the BSB gives it. Psalm 69:25 speaks of 'their place' and 'their tents' in the plural, and Peter says 'his place,' singular, and 'let no one dwell in it.' Peter has narrowed the plural of the enemies of the righteous sufferer to the one who represents them, and combined it with Psalm 109:8, 'May another take his position,' where the Greek word for position or oversight is episkope, a word later used for the office of an overseer. The word translated 'position' has a long history in the church's vocabulary of oversight.

typology.type: The twelve tribes and the twelve apostles
typology.fulfillment: Israel was built from twelve tribes, and Jesus appointed twelve apostles, promising that they would sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel, Luke 22:30. The reconstitution of the Twelve here shows that the new community is the renewed Israel, with the apostles as its foundation. Revelation 21:12 and 14 completes the picture, with the twelve tribes on the gates and the twelve apostles on the foundations. The type escalates in scope: Israel's tribes were a nation, and the apostles are the foundation of a people drawn from every nation, Ephesians 2:20. The correspondence falls short of an identity, since the church is not a replacement of Israel but the enlarged people of God in Christ.

typology.type: The righteous sufferer and his betrayer
typology.fulfillment: David wrote of enemies who repaid his goodness with hatred, and of a close friend who lifted his heel against him, Psalm 41:9, which Jesus applies to Judas in John 13:18. Peter reads Psalms 69 and 109 in the same light, with Judas as the one who stands in the place of David's enemies. The pattern is escalated: David's suffering is partial and his enemies are particular, but Christ's suffering is the full and final case, and Judas's betrayal is the sharpest example. The type falls short because David's psalms are real prayers in David's own circumstances, and the application to Judas is Peter's inspired reading, not their only sense.

typology.type: The lot and the Lord's decision
typology.fulfillment: Israel used the lot to learn God's will about the land, Joshua 18:6 to 10, and about priestly service, 1 Chronicles 24:5. Proverbs 16:33 expresses the theology: 'The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.' In Acts 1 the lot is used for the last time in the Bible, at the threshold of the new age. After the Spirit comes, guidance is inward and communal. The progression shows the movement from external signs under the old covenant to the indwelling Spirit, promised in Ezekiel 36:27. The pattern falls short in that the lot was always a means and never an end, and the Lord who answered it is the one who now guides through His Spirit.

typology.type: The place abandoned and the place filled
typology.fulfillment: Judas left his 'rightful place' and another took his position. There is a pattern in Scripture of a fallen office being taken up by another: Saul rejected and David anointed, 1 Samuel 16:1 and 13, and the faithless priestly house replaced by a faithful priest, 1 Samuel 2:35. In Christ the pattern is completed: the first Adam's failure is answered by the last Adam who does not fail, Romans 5:19. The correspondence is loose, a matter of resonance, since the apostles' circle is filled by an ordinary man chosen to witness, while the true replacement of every failure is the one Lord Jesus.

study.christ:
The whole passage is about securing a witness to Christ. The point of the Twelve was never to have a council of officials but to have men who could say, 'We saw Him, we ate with Him, we know that He rose.' The criterion in verse 22 is 'a witness with us of His resurrection.' The resurrection is not one doctrine among others. It is the fact on which the apostolic message depends, and Paul would say that without it faith is futile, 1 Corinthians 15:14.

Christ is also the Lord who chose them and who is still choosing. The prayer, 'Show us which of these two You have chosen,' addresses Him as one who is present with His church and who directs her. Jesus said in John 15:16 that He chose them, and in Acts 1:2 that He had given instructions to 'the apostles He had chosen.' This is the same Lord who now answers from heaven. The ascended Christ governs His church, and the first example is the filling of the Twelve.

Judas's betrayal is read in light of the Psalms, which means that the betrayer's fate falls within the Scripture's account of the righteous sufferer. Christ is the one in whom that account comes true. The Gospel shows Him knowing the betrayer in advance, John 6:70 and 71 and 13:21 to 27, and Acts shows that even this fell within God's purpose, Acts 2:23. He was not a victim of circumstance.

There is also a quiet portrait of Christ's patience with His people. The apostles who had fled at His arrest, who doubted at His resurrection and who asked about the kingdom right up to the ascension, are the ones He entrusts with His mission. Guard against turning the passage into a proof of apostolic succession in the later sense. The text is about eyewitness testimony to Christ, and it is Christ's own appointment, not a human ladder, that makes the apostles what they are.
study.god:
The prayer of verse 24 gives a short theology of God: He knows every heart, and He chooses. These two attributes belong together. Because God sees what no human election can see, the choice of His servants is His, and the church's part is to seek and submit, not to campaign. The language echoes the Old Testament picture of God who weighs hearts, 1 Samuel 16:7 and 1 Chronicles 28:9, and the New Testament confession that nothing is hidden from Him, Hebrews 4:13.

The passage also shows God's sovereignty over events that look like tragedy. The Holy Spirit 'foretold through the mouth of David' what would happen to Judas, verse 16, and yet Judas is no puppet: he 'abandoned' the ministry and went to 'his rightful place.' Scripture holds both truths at once, as Acts 2:23 does with the cross, 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and 'you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death.' Worship in this light is not a resolution of the mystery but trust in a God whose purposes are not defeated by human sin.

God's way of guiding His people is shown to be through His word and through prayer together. Luke places the Scripture first: Peter begins with 'the Scripture had to be fulfilled.' Then comes the praying community, 'with one accord.' Then a method fit for that moment, and last, a result received as God's. The outline is a kind of liturgy of decision: word, prayer, action and acceptance.

The scene is also a picture of God's faithfulness during waiting. He had told them to wait for the Spirit. Between the promise and the fulfilment there are ten ordinary days, and they are spent in prayer and in tending the community. God does not act only in spectacular moments. He also works through the quiet obedience of a hundred and twenty people in an upstairs room. He is the God who completes what He begins, and who sees that everything is in place when the day of Pentecost arrives.

crossReferences.note: The psalm of a righteous sufferer includes a prayer that his enemies' dwelling be desolate. Peter applies it to Judas, narrowing the plural to the single betrayer. The same psalm is used of Jesus in John 2:17 and in the Passion accounts, so the application belongs to a wider reading of the psalm as speaking of the Messiah.

The psalm asks that the wicked man's days be few and another take his position. Peter reads this as a divine warrant to fill Judas's office. The Greek of the word for position is the later word for oversight, and the verse became a charter for the church's concern that the apostolic circle be complete.

Matthew gives a different angle on the death of Judas, with the thirty pieces of silver returned, the suicide, and the purchase of the Potter's Field by the priests. It shares with Acts 1:18 and 19 the money, the field and the name Field of Blood. The two accounts are best read together.

Jesus spent the night in prayer and then chose twelve whom He named apostles, and the list ends with Judas Iscariot who became a traitor. The choice of Matthias is made against that background: the Lord had chosen the Twelve, and the vacancy is filled by the Lord's own decision.

Jesus promised that the Twelve would sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. This gives the reason for the importance of the number twelve. The apostles are the foundation of the renewed people of God, and the vacancy left by Judas had to be filled for the symbol to stand.

This proverb gives the theology behind the apostles' method: whatever falls out of the lap, the outcome is settled by God and not by chance. They treat the lot as the means by which He shows His choice. Prayer comes before it, and acceptance follows it.

God does not look at what people look at; He looks at the heart. This is the principle that Acts 1:24 appeals to, 'You know everyone's heart.' The church faces a choice between two good men, and only God can see the hearts of both, so they ask Him to show His choice.

In the next account of an appointment in Acts, the church chooses seven men by the congregation's selection after the Spirit has come, with prayer and the laying on of hands. Comparing the two shows the continuity of prayer, and the difference in method after Pentecost.

Paul lists those to whom the risen Lord appeared, including the Twelve and then all the apostles, and finally himself. The list confirms that the circle of the Twelve was understood to be complete and that the witness of the apostles stood at the heart of the gospel.

The new Jerusalem has twelve gates with the names of the twelve tribes, and twelve foundations with the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The completed circle of Acts 1 is a small picture of the people of God in the new creation, built on the apostles' witness.

study.oneStory:
From Genesis on, the Bible's story is about a people God is gathering and a representative figure through whom He acts. Adam failed, and Israel, the son of God, also failed. The twelve tribes were scattered, and the house of David fell. The Gospels announce that God has come to gather the twelve tribes anew around the Messiah, and the choice of twelve apostles is the sign. When one of them falls, the symbol is broken, and Acts 1 repairs it before the new age begins. The story depends not on any person's reliability but on the faithfulness of God who completes His purposes.

The passage also answers a question from the past: how can one of Jesus' own men betray Him, and what does this do to His mission? The answer is that Scripture had foreseen it and that the mission continues. Psalm 41:9, Psalm 69 and Psalm 109 all become windows into God's wisdom. The apostle's testimony will not be undone by the failure of one, and what He started will not be abandoned.

Looking ahead, the filled circle is the base from which the gospel moves out. Pentecost follows at once. The Twelve preach in Jerusalem, and the witness goes to Samaria, to the ends of the earth, and through the whole of Acts. Their testimony is the foundation of the church, Ephesians 2:20, and in the end their names are written on the foundations of the city of God, Revelation 21:14. The upper room with its hundred and twenty is a small seed of that city, a people gathered by the word, praying together, and awaiting the promise of the Father.

quiz.q: What were the believers doing as they waited between the ascension and Pentecost?

options.text: Devoting themselves with one accord to prayer.
options.note: Luke stresses that they continued united in prayer while they waited.

options.text: Gathering together in the upper room.
options.note: True, they gathered in the upper room, but the emphasis is on what they did there: they prayed with one accord.

options.text: Preaching publicly throughout Jerusalem.
options.note: That comes only after Pentecost; before the Spirit came they waited and prayed rather than preaching.

options.text: Arguing over who would be the greatest among them.
options.note: The text shows a united, prayerful community, not one divided by rivalry.

quiz.q: Why did Peter say Judas's place had to be filled?

options.text: Because Scripture foretold it, and a witness of the resurrection was needed to complete the number.
options.note: Peter grounds the decision in the Psalms and in the need for a full circle of eyewitness apostles.

options.text: Because the Psalms said another should take his position.
options.note: True and cited by Peter, but this leaves out the further reason, the need for a witness of the resurrection.

options.text: Because the church wanted to punish Judas by replacing him.
options.note: The motive was not punishment but fulfilling Scripture and restoring the witnessing Twelve.

options.text: Because Jesus had commanded them to elect a new leader immediately.
options.note: There is no such command; Peter reasons from Scripture and the church prays for God's choice.

quiz.q: What was the key qualification for the man who would replace Judas?

options.text: He had accompanied Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension and could witness to the resurrection.
options.note: Apostolic testimony required an eyewitness of the risen Lord.

options.text: He had been with the disciples during Jesus' ministry.
options.note: Close, but the requirement is more precise: an eyewitness all the way to the ascension who can testify to the resurrection.

options.text: He was the most gifted speaker among the believers.
options.note: Eloquence was not the criterion; eyewitness experience of the risen Christ was.

options.text: He came from a prominent family in Jerusalem.
options.note: Social standing had nothing to do with it; the qualification was firsthand witness of Jesus.

quiz.q: How did the church make the final choice between the two men?

options.text: They prayed to the Lord who knows every heart, then cast lots, and it fell to Matthias.
options.note: They asked God to show His choice and trusted Him to direct the lot.

options.text: They cast lots between Joseph and Matthias.
options.note: Accurate about the lot, but it omits the prayer that God would reveal His choice, the heart of the scene.

options.text: They took a majority vote among the hundred and twenty.
options.note: It was decided by lot after prayer, not by a show of hands.

options.text: Peter simply appointed Matthias on his own authority.
options.note: Peter did not choose; the church prayed and the decision was left to God through the lot.

quiz.q: What does this passage show about how the early church made decisions?

options.text: They sought God's will through prayer and Scripture, trusting Him to guide the outcome.
options.note: The church reasons from Scripture and submits the choice to God who knows the heart.

options.text: They followed the practice of casting lots for every decision.
options.note: This is the last recorded instance of casting lots; after Pentecost the Spirit leads, so it is not the abiding pattern.

options.text: They relied on Peter's leadership to settle the matter.
options.note: Peter did lead the discussion, but the decision was submitted to God in prayer, not settled by Peter alone.

options.text: They made choices by their own reasoning without seeking God.
options.note: The opposite is true: prayer and Scripture governed the whole process.

questions: The believers waited together in united prayer before the Spirit came. What does their patience teach you about the place of prayer before action in your own life?
Peter read the painful events around Judas in the light of Scripture. How might Scripture reframe a difficult or confusing situation you are facing right now?
The church asked the Lord who knows every heart to show His choice. Where do you need to stop leaning on your own preference and ask God to guide a decision?
The apostles were valued as witnesses of what they had seen. What have you seen and known of the risen Christ that you could testify to this week?
Judas abandoned a ministry he had shared in, while Matthias took it up. What ministry has God entrusted to you, and are you tending it faithfully?

translationNotes.note: A Sabbath day's journey is explained in a footnote as about 2,000 cubits, roughly 3,000 feet or 914 meters, the distance permitted for travel on the Sabbath.

These verses are Luke's parenthetical explanation for readers, describing the field of blood; the account complements Matthew 27, viewing Judas's end and the purchase of the field from different angles.
Peter quotes Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8, drawing together two psalms of the righteous sufferer and applying them to Judas and to the filling of his place.
